title: Brands Are RL Environments, Part Two
subtitle: The kitchen was the easy world. This time we asked a new model to start a car perfume company from nothing. Over The Air came back, and the hard parts taught us more than the easy ones.

content.text: Ben Thompson wrote a piece last month called The End of the Internet, about how AI is turning the open web into, at best, a battle zone. One line from it has stuck with me, about apps: when anyone can make one, "the surge in slop will make the market worse for everyone." He was talking about software. I think the same thing is about to happen to physical products, and it is already starting.

Walk through any marketplace and you can see it. The same bottle sold under ten brand names. The same lifestyle photo on a hundred listings. Products that were rendered before they were designed, listed before they were sampled, and advertised before anyone held one. AI made it cheap to invent a product page. It did not make it cheaper to make a product worth keeping.

Physical slop is worse than digital slop in one important way: it doesn't scroll away. A bad image costs you a second of attention. A bad product costs you money, then a return, then a box in a landfill, and it teaches the buyer to trust the next listing a little less. If AI is going to help make physical brands, and it clearly is, I want it to make objects people keep rather than ones they send back.
In
part one

of this series I argued that a brand is a reinforcement learning environment, and that slop is what happens when nobody designs that environment on purpose. We tested the idea by asking a new model, post-trained by the Sloosh team, to start a cloud kitchen from nothing. It came back with Pam's Kitchen: one pot a day, forty pieces, one voice.

A kitchen, though, is a kind world to learn in. The episodes are short; you know by 9pm whether people locked tomorrow's pot. Mistakes cost a pot of dal. So for the second test we picked a harder world on purpose.
We asked the same model to start a car perfume company.

attrs.alt: The OTA Shifter: a carbon knob, a fluted glass body, a steel vent.

content.text: The OTA Shifter: a carbon knob, a fluted glass body, a steel vent.

It came back with Over The Air, or OTA for short. Two objects: a scent shaped like a gear knob, called the Shifter, and a scent that sits in your cupholder. A website that plays like a car film. A brand book with every rule written down, built around a logo traced from a car vent.

The pieces are good, and I'll show you all of them. But the more interesting story is what changes when the environment is a physical product, because almost every assumption that made the kitchen easy stops being true.
The Easy World and the Hard World

Start with a quick refresher. In RL, an agent sees the state of an environment, takes an action, and gets a reward; over many episodes it builds up a policy, a habit of taking the actions that get rewarded. Coding models got good this way because code has a crisp, cheap, automatic reward: did the tests pass?

Brands have no test suite, which is why part one leaned on manufactured rewards: a critic model with a rubric, dense signals like WhatsApp locks, and human taste acting as the reward model. In the kitchen that worked well because the real world gave fast feedback on top. Every night was an episode.
A car perfume breaks that in three ways.

First, the reward is slow. You cannot A/B test a mould overnight. The object has to be sampled, tooled, filled, packed and shipped before anyone can buy it, which means the sale sits months up the road.
Second, mistakes are expensive. A bad pot of dal costs a pot of dal. A bad mould costs a year of stock sitting in a warehouse.

Third, and most important, the gap between simulation and reality is wide. RL researchers call this the sim-to-real gap; it is the reason robots that walk beautifully in simulation fall over in the lab. For a product, the simulation is the render, and renders lie. Carbon on a screen is not carbon in daylight. Fluted glass looks perfect in a render and shows every fingerprint in your hand.
If an RL-style approach can build a good brand in this world, it can probably build one anywhere. If it can't, we would learn where the edges are. Either result was worth having.
Same Stack, Different World

The method was the same as the kitchen. You start with nothing. Then you lay on top of that the right skill files, models, workflows, brand sections, insights, guides, methodologies, and your own taste. Then you put it together.

What I didn't expect was how differently the layers got stressed. The kitchen leaned on insights and voice; the brand was mostly words. The car leaned on constraints and materials; the brand was mostly objects. Let me walk through it.
Start with nothing
In the kitchen, "nothing" was a mess of three menus. In the car, nothing was a feeling: car fresheners are sad.

A car is a little room you spend hours in. Commutes, road trips, traffic. For a lot of people it is the only private space they get all day, and they spend real money on it. Sound got premium speakers. Light got ambient LEDs. Touch got alcantara and heated seats. Smell got a cardboard tree hanging off the mirror.

That is the starting state, and when you see a state like that you know where the reward is: in the gap. But the gap is also a trap. The obvious move, "luxury car freshener," is a slop generator all by itself. Gold foil, black boxes, fake French words, a tree that costs more.

It is worth asking why the category defaults to slop in the first place, because the answer is the same reward problem as everywhere else. A car freshener is sold at a petrol station counter or in a marketplace grid, so the reward it has historically chased is the impulse grab: a bright colour, a big claim, a price that makes it a non-decision. Nobody optimised for how it feels to live with the thing for three months, because nobody was rewarded for that. The cardboard tree is not a design failure. It is a perfectly trained policy for the wrong reward.
So the first job of the environment was to push past the obvious, and it did that by changing the question.
What if a car scent looked like it belonged in the car?

Not hung off it, not clipped to it, but part of it. That question did for the car what "one pot a day" did for the kitchen: it shrank the action space. The agent was no longer designing "a perfume." It was designing an object that belongs in a cabin, and every later choice had to answer to that.
Skill files

For a physical product, the skill files teach different things. How objects actually get made. How to think about scale in millimetres. How to light a macro shot of carbon weave. And, most importantly, how to describe a product without adjectives.

That last rule is my favourite in this whole project. Luxury brands talk in materials: carbon, glass, steel, air. Cheap brands talk in adjectives: premium, elegant, exquisite, sophisticated. A skill file that says "name the material, skip the adjective" kills half the slop in this category before it is written.
Models

The kitchen needed writers, food photographers and a critic. The car needed one more thing: a model that thinks in three dimensions, for renders, cutaways and scale shots. And it needed a very particular critic, one that knows what cheap looks like.

That critic asks one question of every render: would this look like plastic in your hand? Glossy chrome that reads as a toy is killed. Glass that reads as an acrylic block is killed. Carbon that reads as a printed sticker is killed. The full rubric had five questions: Would this look like plastic? Is a real material named? Is there a real size, in millimetres? Could a petrol-station brand have made this? Does it belong in a car? The fourth question does the most work.

Workflows

The kitchen's order was ritual, name, menu, site, print. The car went insight, object, ritual, name, film, brand book, and the difference was deliberate. For a physical product, the shape is the brand, so the object came before the name. If you name it first, you end up designing to fit a word.

The workflow also followed a cost curriculum: cheap things first, expensive things last. Words cost nothing, so the insight and the one-line idea came first. Renders cost a little, so the object was explored in pixels next, dozens of knobs and cups. Film costs more, so it was only made once the object settled. Samples cost the most, so they come last, and only for the winners.
Insights
This is where the car brand got good.
One insight drove the whole product: put it where the hand already goes.

Fresheners hang off the mirror or clip to a vent, where you never touch them. You forget them, and they die quietly in a corner. OTA goes where your hand already rests, the gear stick and the cupholder. You touch it without thinking, so the scent becomes a habit.

attrs.alt: Two objects, where your hand already goes.

content.text: Two objects, where your hand already goes.

The Shifter is a gear-knob-shaped scent that sits in the cupholder, about 110 mm tall, with a 46 mm carbon knob, a fluted glass body and a steel vent. The Cup is a cupholder scent a little taller than a can. And there is a wink in the Shifter: more and more cars no longer have a real gear stick. Electric cars and automatics have dials and buttons. OTA gives you one back, as a perfume. Car people won't say they miss the gear stick, but they smile when they see one. That is an insight no dataset gives you. It comes from sitting in cars with people who love them, and noticing what they reach for.

attrs.alt: The Shifter in a cupholder, at dusk.

content.text: The Shifter in a cupholder, at dusk.
The second insight gave the name. Modern cars update "over the air": new features land overnight, without a trip to the garage. Car people know that phrase cold. And scent travels through air.

attrs.alt: The name: scent travels through air; cars update over the air.

content.text: The name: scent travels through air; cars update over the air.

A name like this can be scored on four checks. Does it say what it does? Does it sit in the category, where buyers already say "air"? Do car people know the phrase? Does it shorten well? Most candidate names pass one or two. Over The Air passed all four, and it shortens to three letters that look good on a vent.
Guides
For the kitchen, the guides were dish stories. For the car, the guides were scenes.

Car people love car films: the slow reveal, the pan across a headlight, the macro on stitching, the engine note before you see the car. So the guides were frames from that world: black backgrounds, one light source, one word on screen, materials before features. The model learned that grammar, and then built the website as a film.

attrs.alt: Over The Air, Film 01: The Shifter.

content.text: Over The Air, Film 01: The Shifter.
The site opens like a car commercial and cuts between close-ups as you scroll. One word per scene, white type on a black world.
Carbon. 46 mm knob, 2x2 twill.
Air. Perforated steel vent.

Each word is a material, not a feature. Left alone, most models want to explain a product: features, benefits, a tagline, a call to action. The guides pull the other way, toward saying less and showing more, which is a strange thing to have to teach a machine built out of words. You learn what it is made of before you learn what it does, which is how luxury talks. You cannot write "be cinematic" in a skill file; that produces slop. You show twenty cinematic frames and let the model learn the grammar.

It is worth tracing one of those frames through every layer, roughly, because it shows how the stack works on a single piece. Take the Carbon shot. It starts as a black frame. The skill file says how macro shots work: one light, raking across the surface, show texture, hide the edges. The model renders many versions; the weave is too big in some, too shiny in others, and a few have a rainbow sheen that screams plastic. The insight layer pushes the angle: car people know carbon and can spot a fake weave in a second, so the twill has to be right, a real 2x2 pattern. The guide sets the tone: black world, one word, white type. The brand section limits the colour: no orange in this frame, because the orange is saved. The critic asks whether it would look like plastic in your hand, and most versions fail there. A human picks one and writes the caption: 46 mm knob, 2x2 twill. A number and a weave, and no adjective anywhere. Car people read it and nod.
Methodologies
This is where the car world gets hard, because this is the reward.

In the kitchen, the dense rewards sat close to the sale: locks by 9pm, repeat lockers. For a car perfume, the sale is far up the road, so the dense rewards sit further back. Do people watch the film to the end? Do they scroll back to the Shifter? Do they sign up to hear when it ships? Do they share the pull-to-start moment? Do car people in forums say "I want one"?

And for the object itself, the rewards come from hands. Does a prototype feel heavy enough? Does the glass feel cold? Does the pull feel satisfying? Those signals are expensive; each one costs a sample. So you don't get many, and this is exactly where the sim-to-real gap bites.

In simulation, you can run a thousand episodes in an afternoon: renders, mockups, critic scores. In reality you get a handful: a few prototypes, a few people holding them. And reality disagrees with the renders a lot.

So the methodology had one firm rule: the hand beats the render. When a real person holding a sample disagrees with the critic, the critic gets updated, not the person. That is how you close a sim-to-real gap without a robotics lab: lots of cheap simulated episodes to explore, a few expensive real ones to correct, and a critic that learns from both.

Robotics has a useful trick for this that translates surprisingly well. When OpenAI trained a robot hand to solve a Rubik's cube in 2019, a big part of getting it to work in the real world was domain randomization: they trained it across simulations with varied physics, lighting and appearances, so that reality looked like just one more variation. The equivalent for a product is to render every candidate under many conditions, not just the flattering one: harsh noon light, a dirty cupholder, a fingerprint on the glass, a cheap phone camera. A design that only looks good in its hero render is fragile. A design that survives a hundred unflattering renders is much more likely to survive a real hand.

Car designers, it is worth noting, worked this out decades ago. A car studio is an RL environment run by humans. Designers sketch hundreds of cars; the best few become full-size clay models in a room with good light; senior people walk around the clay, crouch, squint and touch it; most models die, a few come back changed. Sketches are the simulation, clay is the reality check, and the review is the reward. What is new is the speed of the sketch phase. A model can explore more shapes before lunch than a studio could in a month. The clay review still matters, maybe more than ever.
The Shifter, sealed.
The gift box.
Brand sections, and the art of cutting
The biggest single win in the OTA project was a cut.

The first version of the brand book had a lot of ideas: a lamp-counter wordmark, fluted glass as a graphic device, five headlight drawings. Every one of them was fine. Together they were noise. So the second version retired all of them, and the slat, taken from a car vent, became the only device.

In RL terms this is the switch from exploration to exploitation. Early on, you want an agent to try a lot, because exploration is how good ideas get found. Then you have to stop, pick the one that works, and use it everywhere, because exploitation is how a good idea becomes a brand.

Models are great explorers and bad at stopping. Most AI brand work never makes the switch: every new asset gets a fresh idea, which is why AI-made brands so often feel like a mood board, lots of nice things and no identity. Stopping is a taste call, so the environment has to hold the brakes. After this project, ours does: after three devices, the critic asks which one to retire.

The product itself went through the same thing. Along the way the model explored very different objects: an oak sphere with an amber shift gate, a home dock with a light line around its base, a black-and-steel knob with a domed window.
Directions explored along the way.
The carbon Shifter is what survived the cut.
Taste, as an artifact
The eighth layer is your own taste, and for OTA it showed up in a very literal way.

The logo started as a hand sketch of a car vent, horizontal slats, with the letters O, T and A built from the same slats. The most important rule in the brand book is three words long: traced, not redrawn.

attrs.alt: From a car vent to a wordmark. Traced, not redrawn.

content.text: From a car vent to a wordmark. Traced, not redrawn.

The original sketch was kept exactly, every slat and every gap, and then cleaned into vectors. That matters because when a model "improves" a sketch, it averages it. It straightens the wobble, evens out the gaps, and makes it look like every other geometric logo. It loses the soul.

This is also where honesty matters most. A brand that redraws its own origin to look more polished is telling a small lie about where it came from. So the sketch became a hard constraint. The agent was not allowed to touch it; it could only build around it. RL has a name for this too, a constrained action space: some moves are simply off the table. In robotics, it's "don't walk through the wall." In brands, it's "don't redraw the founder's sketch."

I think this is the most underrated idea in the whole stack. Your taste does not have to be a vague vibe. It can be an artifact: a sketch, a photo, a paragraph written at midnight, a folder of screenshots you are jealous of. Lock it in place and let the model build the world around it. Most founders already have that folder in their camera roll. It just never reaches the model.

The rest of the marks grew from the one sketch: the wordmark, a box mark, the O alone as a favicon, a lockup on carbon. And they came with proper rules: clear space is half the wordmark height; the wordmark is never smaller than 24 px on screen or 7 mm in print.
The marks, with clear space.

Even motion got rules, and they are worth reading because they show how far an environment can carry taste. The slats arrive from the left, one row at a time, forty milliseconds apart, travelling for 480 milliseconds on a custom ease curve. Then a single orange streak crosses once, in 900 milliseconds, like a tail light passing at night. None of those numbers came from a model's sense of what looks nice. They came from a human deciding what the brand should feel like in motion, and then writing it down precisely enough that any model, or any designer, can reproduce it every time. That is what turning taste into an environment looks like at the smallest scale: a feeling, made into numbers, made into a rule.
One Tail Light
The palette deserves its own section, because it is the cleanest example of reward hacking I have seen in a brand, and the cleanest fix.

attrs.alt: Concrete, carbon and one tail light.

content.text: Concrete, carbon and one tail light.

The palette is a car park at night: carbon, asphalt, gunmetal, concrete, fog, paper. Greys, mostly. And then one orange, called Signal, used rarely, like a tail light. That restraint is what makes it feel premium. Loud brands shout everywhere; premium brands whisper, then flash once.

Now think about that orange as a reward problem. An agent rewarded on attention will use more orange, because orange gets clicks: orange buttons, orange banners, orange everything. A week later the brand looks like a discount store. That is the CoastRunners boat from part one again, a cheap signal eating the real goal.

So the methodology carries a penalty: every extra use of orange costs points. Orange is allowed once per screen, and the critic counts. It sounds silly to write a rule about one colour. It is the difference between a brand and a poster.
Putting It Together
Everything in OTA hangs off one line, the way everything in the kitchen hung off "one pot a day." For the car, the line is: it belongs in the car.

The objects sit where your hand goes. The name comes from how cars update. The logo is a vent. The palette is a car park at night. The film talks like a car commercial. And the ritual feels like starting the engine.
Pull to start.

Every good product has a ritual: opening an iPhone box, popping a champagne cork. OTA's is pull to start. You pull the knob up and the scent opens, a small moment that feels like starting the car. Pull, release, breathe. Rituals make a product feel alive, and they are easy to film, which makes them easy to share, which is a dense reward again. The ritual is also a product decision, not just a marketing one. The pull has to feel right: too loose and it feels cheap, too stiff and it feels broken. That feel cannot be judged in a render. It is one of those precious real episodes, a sample in a hand and a face that lights up or doesn't, and it is exactly the kind of reward the environment cannot manufacture on its own.

attrs.alt: The Shifter, with the car it belongs in.

content.text: The Shifter, with the car it belongs in.

attrs.alt: Film still: the car and the scent.

content.text: Film still: the car and the scent.
And then the applications go everywhere a vent can go: packaging, caps, tees, keyrings, all passing the same rules. Slats, greys, one orange, materials over adjectives.

attrs.alt: On everything you can put a vent on.

content.text: On everything you can put a vent on.
The product, at real scale.
The First Ninety Days

If I were running the first ninety days of OTA, I would watch a small dashboard, the same way I described for the kitchen, but tilted toward the slow world: how many people finish the film, how many scroll back to the Shifter, waitlist sign-ups by city, pull-to-start clips shared, car forum threads that mention it, and sample feedback in people's own words.

Each one is a breadcrumb; none is a sale. But each can move the environment. If the Cup gets more love than the Shifter, the story shifts toward the Cup. If people hate the fingerprints on fluted glass, the material shifts. If nobody finishes the film, the film gets shorter. The street trains the critic, the critic trains the renders, the renders become samples, and the samples meet hands again.
Can It Move Sales?

The second half of the question I asked in part one was whether an environment like this can build something that sells, not just something that looks good. For a physical product, that means the environment has to think like a shop, and the craft choices have to answer to reasons people buy.

Look at where the money could come from. Gifting, first: car people are hard to buy for, and a gear knob that smells good is an easy yes, so the packaging has to feel like a gift. Refills, second: scent runs out, which is a natural reason to come back, so the glass and the vent have to be easy to refill, and the ritual repeats along with the sale. Car culture, third: meets, forums and detailing shops are places where people already spend on their cars, and a product that looks like a car part fits in there in a way a cardboard tree never could.

Each of those is a reward the environment can aim at. Gift-worthiness gets scored. Refill ease gets scored. "Would this sit on a detailing shop counter?" gets scored. That is how craft connects to sales: not by adding a discount badge, but by making every craft choice answer to a reason to buy.
Integration, All the Way Down
There is a version of this argument that goes further, and I think it is where physical brands are headed.

In part one I borrowed Ben Thompson's framing of integration and modularity: value flows to the integrated parts of a value chain and away from the modular ones. For digital brands, the integrated part is the environment, while the models are increasingly swappable. For physical products, the environment has to reach further down, into how things are actually made.

Today, most of OTA's environment stops at the render and the sample. The skill files know about millimetres and materials, but not about wall thickness for blown glass, draft angles on a moulded cap, or what a supplier's minimum order looks like. That knowledge lives with manufacturers and a few experienced product designers, and the brand only meets it when a sample comes back wrong.

The obvious next step is to write that knowledge into the environment too: manufacturing constraints as skill files, supplier quirks as guides, cost and lead time as part of the critic's rubric. At that point the model is no longer just exploring shapes that look good; it is exploring shapes that can be made, at a cost that works, in the time you have. The sim-to-real gap shrinks because the simulation knows more about reality.
That is the same pattern as the kitchen, one level deeper. The more of the real world you write into the environment, the less the model has to guess, and the less room there is for slop.
Same Stack, Different Stress
Put the two experiments side by side and a pattern shows up.

The kitchen leaned on insights and voice; the car leaned on constraints and materials. The kitchen had fast rewards, every night; the car had slow, expensive rewards from hands and samples. The kitchen learned from the street daily; the car learned mostly in simulation, and corrected itself in a few precious real moments. And both had the same enemy, reward hacking, the cheap signal that eats the brand. Fake discounts in one world. Too much orange in the other.
Try a thought experiment: pull one layer out at a time and watch what breaks.

Drop the skill files and the adjectives come back. Drop the insights and the product goes back on the mirror. Drop the guides and the film becomes a stock perfume ad on a beach. Drop the critic and the renders look like plastic, which nobody notices until the sample arrives. Drop the constraints and the logo gets "improved" while the orange spreads everywhere. Drop your taste and everything is fine, and nothing is yours. Every layer holds up a wall, and slop rushes in through whichever one you pull.

The Cup taught a quieter lesson. It is the simpler object, a scent that sits in the cupholder, a little taller than a can, and it has no gear-knob wink to lean on. Without a clever story to hide behind, it has to win on material and feel alone. That made it a good test of the critic, because plastic looks like plastic when there is nothing else to look at. Simple objects are honest that way, and they are where a weak environment shows first.

If you want to try this on a physical product of your own, start tiny. Pick one object you love that has a sad version in the world: a pen, a water bottle, a key holder. Write the one question that shrinks it, the way "what if it belonged in the car?" shrank OTA. Write five banned words and five real materials. Find twenty frames you wish you had shot. Draw one rough sketch and lock it. Then ask a model to explore inside that box, render every candidate under ugly light as well as pretty light, kill most of what comes back, and write down why. In a week you will have the beginnings of an environment, and you will notice the drafts getting better, not because the model changed, but because the world around it did.
Where This Leaves Us

The model is the least interesting part of all this. It is very good now: fast, patient, and inside a good environment it holds every rule at once, the millimetres, the orange, the banned words, in a way a tired human does not by Friday afternoon. But a great model in a bad environment makes slop, and a good model in a great environment makes brands. The environment is the product.

There are honest limits, and the car makes them clearer than the kitchen did. The physical world is slower: moulds, suppliers and samples still take the time they take, and no model skips that. Renders lie, and always will, so you budget for real samples and treat every real hand as a precious episode. And taste stays human. The sketch came from a person. The "yes, that's the one" came from a person. The model made everything around it faster; it did not decide what was beautiful. That is the split I want: models for speed and patience, people for taste and judgement, and an environment that holds both.

It is also why this is what we are building at ShopOS: an AI lab that rolls up creative studios, so the internet isn't full of slop. Great studios are great environments. Writing them down, and letting them run at the speed of software, is how you get more Pam's Kitchens and Over The Airs, and fewer cardboard trees.
The model didn't get more creative. The environment made creativity the winning move.
p.s. Pull to start.
